questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How to build your own chatbot at home
Why we shouldn't trust chatbots too much
The history of computer games and AI
How banks use technology to save money
questions.why: They discuss whether chatbots think for themselves and why it's dangerous to always trust them.

questions.q: How do modern chatbots produce their answers?
options: They search for the answer in a large dictionary
A human writes the answers quickly
They predict the next likely word, one after another
They copy answers from other users
questions.why: Neil says the technology predicts the next word likely to be used in a sentence.

questions.q: Where has Rob used chatbots himself?
options: When writing essays for his university course
When talking to his bank or booking tickets
When asking for medical advice at night
When chatting to his friends and family
questions.why: Rob says he has used them when talking to his bank or booking a ticket on a website.

questions.q: According to Professor Emily M Bender, what mistake do people often make?
options: They think fluent text must be reliable
They ask chatbots far too many questions
They think chatbots are too slow to be useful
They refuse to try any new technology
questions.why: She says we tend to react to fluent, coherent text as authoritative and reliable, but ChatGPT's text is none of that.

options: That chatbots will suddenly stop working
That people will soon get bored of chatbots
That chatbots will replace all school teachers
That chatbots may soon know more than we do
questions.why: He said chatbots could soon overtake the level of information a human brain holds.

questions.q: According to Professor Bender, why might a chatbot say things that sound like it has feelings?
options: Because it really does have human feelings
Because its makers want to trick the users
Because it replies with likely words
Because it has learned to copy animals
questions.why: She says if you ask it how it feels, you can provoke it to say things a sentient being would say.

questions.q: What does Professor Bender say about humans and language?
options: We imagine a mind behind any language
We understand machines better than people
We learn languages best from computers
We only trust language that is spoken
questions.why: She says 'we are really primed to imagine a mind behind language'.

questions.q: What is Rob's view of chatbots at the end?
options: They can become good friends
They are smarter than people
They should be banned
They are just machines, not friends
questions.why: Rob says, 'they are not your friend, they are just machines!'
